question: Why should I write tests before refactoring?
text:
Writing tests before refactoring gives you a safety net that captures the *current* behavior of the code, bugs and all. Since refactoring is supposed to change structure without changing behavior, you need a fast, reliable way to verify that nothing shifted — tests let you make changes and get immediate feedback, rather than relying on manual inspection or hoping you didn't break anything.

Without this net, refactoring becomes guesswork: you can't distinguish "I improved the design" from "I silently changed what the code does." Tests also clarify the existing contract of the code before you touch it, forcing you to understand edge cases and inputs you might otherwise overlook. In short, tests turn refactoring from a risky rewrite into a controlled, verifiable transformation.

question: Why does sleep matter for learning?
text:
Sleep plays an active role in learning, not just a passive recovery period. During sleep—particularly slow-wave and REM stages—the brain replays and reorganizes the neural activity from the day's experiences, a process called memory consolidation. This strengthens the connections between neurons that encode new information, effectively transferring memories from a fragile, short-term state in the hippocampus into more stable, long-term storage in the cortex. Without adequate sleep, newly learned material is more likely to be forgotten or poorly integrated with existing knowledge.

Sleep also prepares the brain to learn new things in the first place. Studies show that sleep deprivation impairs the hippocampus's ability to encode new information, so even before any forgetting occurs, a tired brain simply absorbs less. Additionally, sleep supports creative problem-solving and insight by allowing the brain to find novel connections between unrelated pieces of information—something that's much harder to do when awake and alert on too little rest. In short, sleep both locks in what you've learned and primes you to learn effectively the next day.

question: How do I decide between renting and buying a bike?
text:
Cost usually decides it fast: if you'd ride fewer than a few times a month, renting (or bike-share) is cheaper since buying means paying for a bike, maintenance, and storage you barely use. If you expect to ride regularly — commuting, frequent errands, or training — buying pays off within a few months and gives you a bike fit to your body and needs, which rentals rarely offer.

Beyond cost, think about convenience and commitment. Renting is great for trying out a style (road, gravel, e-bike) before committing, for travel, or for occasional use without worrying about theft or upkeep. Buying makes sense once you know what you want, value having it ready anytime, and don't mind handling repairs or secure storage. If you're unsure, renting a few times first is a low-risk way to find out before buying.

question: Why does a team need version control?
text:
A team needs version control because it gives everyone a shared, reliable history of how code changes over time. Without it, people overwrite each other's work, lose track of what changed and why, and have no easy way to recover a working version after a bad change. Version control (like Git) solves this by tracking every change with who made it and why, letting multiple people work on the same codebase in parallel without stepping on each other.

Beyond history, version control enables safe collaboration through branching and merging—developers can experiment or build features in isolation, then integrate their work once it's ready, with tools to resolve conflicts cleanly. It also supports accountability and review (via commit messages and pull requests), makes it possible to roll back to any previous state if something breaks, and serves as the backbone for CI/CD pipelines that automatically test and deploy code. In short, it turns software development from a fragile, single-person activity into a coordinated, auditable team process.

question: ¿Por qué conviene escribir pruebas antes de refactorizar?
text:
Escribir pruebas antes de refactorizar funciona como una red de seguridad: capturan el comportamiento actual del código (incluyendo casos borde que quizás ni recuerdes que existen) antes de tocar la estructura interna. Así, cualquier cambio que rompa algo se detecta de inmediato, y puedes distinguir con certeza entre "cambié el diseño pero el comportamiento sigue igual" y "accidentalmente alteré la lógica".

Además, esto fuerza una separación clara entre dos actividades que es peligroso mezclar: cambiar el comportamiento y cambiar la estructura. Si refactorizas sin pruebas y algo falla luego, no sabes si el error estaba ya latente, si lo introdujo el refactor, o si es un cambio de comportamiento no intencional. Con pruebas previas, cada paso del refactor se valida contra un contrato fijo, lo que permite avanzar con confianza y en pasos pequeños y reversibles.

question: ¿Por qué dormir bien ayuda a aprender?
text:
Dormir bien ayuda a aprender porque durante el sueño —especialmente en las fases profundas y en el sueño REM— el cerebro consolida la memoria: transfiere información de almacenamiento temporal (hipocampo) a redes de almacenamiento más estable (corteza), y fortalece las conexiones sinápticas relevantes mientras elimina las que no se usaron. Básicamente, lo aprendido durante el día se "fija" mientras dormimos, lo que mejora la retención a largo plazo.

Además, el sueño insuficiente afecta la atención, la concentración y la capacidad de procesar información nueva al día siguiente, lo que dificulta aprender desde el inicio. Por eso dormir bien no solo ayuda a retener lo ya aprendido, sino que también prepara al cerebro para absorber mejor nueva información.

question: ¿Cómo decidir entre arrendar o comprar una bicicleta?
text:
Depende sobre todo de cuánto y con qué frecuencia vas a usarla. Si es para un uso ocasional —un paseo de vez en cuando o probar si el ciclismo te gusta— arrendar tiene sentido: evitas el desembolso inicial grande, no te preocupas por mantenimiento, robos ni almacenamiento, y puedes probar distintos modelos antes de comprometerte. El arriendo también es mejor si necesitas la bici solo por un período corto (un viaje, una temporada) o si vives en un lugar donde guardarla de forma segura es difícil.

Si en cambio planeas usarla regularmente —para ir al trabajo, entrenar o hacer rutas largas con frecuencia— comprar suele ser más económico a mediano y largo plazo, porque el costo acumulado de arrendar termina superando el precio de compra. Comprar también te da la ventaja de personalizar la bici a tu gusto y tenerla siempre disponible sin depender de la disponibilidad de arriendo. En resumen: para uso esporádico o de prueba, arrienda; para uso frecuente y a largo plazo, compra.

question: ¿Por qué un equipo necesita control de versiones?

Esto reduce conflictos, mejora la colaboración y hace posible procesos como revisión de código antes de integrar cambios, lo cual aumenta la calidad y estabilidad del software.

question: Why should I write tests before refactoring?
text:
Tests before refactoring give you a safety net. You capture the current, correct behavior as a set of checks, so when you restructure the code, you can tell quickly whether you changed what it does or only how it does it. Without that net, a refactor can quietly break something, and you won't find out until much later, when it's harder to trace back to the change that caused it.

They also force you to clarify what the code is actually supposed to do before you touch it. Writing a test means naming inputs, outputs, and edge cases explicitly, which often reveals ambiguity or hidden assumptions in the existing implementation. That clarity makes the refactor itself easier, since you're reshaping code whose contract you already understand, rather than guessing at it mid-edit.

question: Why should I write tests before refactoring?

If you don't have tests, you can't actually tell whether you refactored or just rewrote the feature with new bugs. A good test suite turns "I think this still works" into "I know this still works," which is what lets you move fast without being reckless.

question: Why does sleep matter for learning?
text:
Sleep consolidates what you learned during the day. While you sleep, the brain replays and strengthens new memories, moving them from short-term storage into longer-term networks. Skip sleep and that process gets cut short, so facts and skills you practiced stay fragile and fade faster.

Sleep also clears the way for new learning. Deep sleep restores attention and working memory, both needed to take in information the next day. Without enough sleep, you can still study, but you retain less and react slower.

question: How do I decide between renting and buying a bike?

Buy if you'll ride weekly or need it for a commute. A decent bike pays for itself within months compared to repeated rental fees, and you gain the convenience of having it ready whenever you want. The tradeoff is upfront cost plus maintenance and storage — so buying makes sense only once your usage is steady enough to justify owning one.

question: Why does a team need version control?
text:
A team needs version control because multiple people change the same files, and without a shared history those changes collide, overwrite each other, or vanish. Version control tracks who changed what and when, lets you merge work from different people, and gives you a safe way to undo a bad change.

It also removes the need to coordinate by hand. Instead of emailing files back and forth or freezing work while one person edits, each person branches, commits, and merges on their own schedule. The real cost without it: lost work, duplicated effort, and no record of why a decision was made.

question: Why does a team need version control?

It also lets people work in parallel without blocking each other. Branches let you try an idea without touching the main codebase, and merging brings the work back together once it's ready. If something breaks, you roll back to a known good state instead of guessing what changed.
